text: said "Drinking cold water makes spicy food burn worse" but capsaicin dissolves in fat, not water: water only fails to wash it away and can spread it; milk or yogurt carry it off
title 'Why Cold Water Fails Against Spicy Food 🌶️🥛' overstated: The narration is scientifically accurate, but the description needed hashtags removed to meet the strict format requirements.

title 'The Only Food That Lasts Forever 🐝✨' overstated: The title is technically an overstatement since other foods like salt and white rice also last forever, but the narration is scientifically sound.

said "which saved early zebras from deadly tropical diseases." but While zebras are susceptible to diseases, the primary evolutionary advantage of stripes is preventing fly landings, which reduces energy expenditure and stress rather than directly preventing the transmission of specific fatal tropic

title 'Why Heat Treating Makes Steel Hard 💪' overstated: The original description claims steel is 'unbreakable', which is an overstatement since quenched steel becomes brittle rather than unbreakable.

Title: Why Your Arms Never Prune -> Arms do prune if submerged long enough, as skin everywhere on the hands and feet can wrinkle, and even limbs can show wrinkling in extreme conditions. The title uses an absolute 'Never' which is false.

Your arms lack these specialized grip pathways. -> The skin on arms does not wrinkle because it lacks the high concentration of sweat ducts found on fingers and toes, where the nervous response creates the folds, not entirely separate 'grip pathways'.

said "Without enough solar heat out there to vaporize ice into glowing comet tails, a second, wider belt was hiding in the dark." but Comets do not need to be close to the Sun to have tails; they develop comas and tails when their ices sublimate as they approach perihelion. Your brain learns to associate the bitterness with the caffeine kick. -> This is a simplified psychological model (conditioned taste preference/learned safety) but is not proven as the sole mechanism; individual differences and the social context of coffee consumption play a major role.
leaving the cream behind on the hotter side. -> The cream's adhesion is not determined by temperature (hotter side), but by the manufacturing process where the first wafer is pressed into the cream.
Nobody cracked it yet, so here is your turn. -> The MIT study explicitly concluded that the distribution is caused by the manufacturing process where one wafer is applied before the other.

The wing edges create aerodynamic noise rather than a cracking sound. -> Wing edges do generate aerodynamic noise, but the statement that they produce no cracking sound is oversimplified; some birds can produce brief popping noises from wing feathers.
That outer hull is incredibly strong. -> The hull is relatively strong compared with other grains, but "incredibly" is an exaggeration.
Other grains like wheat or oats have a porous hull. -> Wheat and oats have a less airtight, more permeable hull rather than a truly porous one.

When they heat up, the steam escapes slowly through these pores instead of building up pressure. -> Moisture can escape because the hull is more permeable and the grains have lower internal moisture (~10% or less).

Zebras and horses split about two to three million years ago from a common ancestor. -> Genetic evidence suggests the divergence occurred significantly earlier, typically cited between 4 and 5 million years ago.
Only the zebra kept its distinct stripes. -> This implies stripes were the ancestral state for both, but it is more likely that stripes evolved specifically within the zebra lineage after the split.

Ever thought why donkeys kept leg stripes while horses lost them? -> The question implies horses once had stripes and lost them. There is no evidence that the ancestor of the modern horse possessed zebra-like body stripes.

Most stars like this pulse in seconds. -> Most detected pulsars have periods measured in milliseconds to a few seconds; stating they 'pulse in seconds' implies a slow rate and ignores the vast majority of millisecond pulsars.

Current models suggest it shouldn't have enough power to produce these waves. -> This is ambiguous. Models (like the 'death line' theory) suggest pulsars should stop emitting when they slow down, but this is a specific theoretical boundary, not a lack of general 'power'.

The leading theory is that this pulsar has an exceptionally strong magnetic field. -> For long-period pulsars, the leading theory is often the opposite: that they have unusually high magnetic fields, but the phrasing implies this is a universal consensus on all 'slow' emitters, which is still an are
